showerhead.title: Showerhead Test
showerhead.short: Measure your shower's water flow and uncover savings potential.

intro.videoAlt: Animation: water filling a measuring cup under a showerhead
details: Use a container of known volume – e.g. a measuring cup or bucket with a 5-litre mark.
Turn on the shower the way you normally shower (usual temperature and strength).
Hold the container fully under the stream and start the stopwatch at the same time.
Stop the time exactly when the water reaches the mark.
Tip: measure two or three times and take the average for a more accurate result.
With an instantaneous water heater: let it run briefly until the temperature is stable.

run.litersInfo: The volume of your container. Standard is 5 litres.
run.secondsInfo: The time in seconds until the container was full.

result.sourceNote: Estimated for hot water via {{source}}. More accurate with your price set.

summary.good: Very efficient – your showerhead uses little water.
summary.medium: Medium usage – there's still savings potential.
summary.high: High usage – a water-saving insert pays off.

fridge.title: Fridge Check
fridge.short: Check the temperature and energy use of your fridge.

intro.imageAlt: Illustration: person measuring the temperature inside the fridge
steps: Put a thermometer in the fridge
details: Place the thermometer in the middle of the fridge – ideally in a glass of water, which shows the real storage temperature.
Close the door and wait several hours (overnight is best) before reading it.
Recommended: 5–7 °C in the fridge and about −18 °C in the freezer compartment.
Every degree colder than necessary noticeably increases electricity use.
While you're at it, check the door seal – if it no longer closes tightly, the appliance cools far more than needed.

run.hint: Rule of thumb: each 1 °C warmer (towards 7 °C) saves ~6% electricity. Turn the dial down and re-measure after a few hours.
run.energyHint: Plug an energy-cost meter between socket and fridge: read the accumulated kWh and runtime (hours) before and after the change.

method.delta: From the achieved temperature difference (~6% per °C).
method.estimate: Potential of setting it to 7 °C (~6% per °C) – not adjusted yet.

status.tooCold: Set too cold – this wastes electricity.

standby.title: Standby Check
standby.short: Track down hidden power drains in standby mode.

intro.needs: You'll need a power meter (energy cost meter).
intro.imageAlt: Illustration: person measuring a TV's standby power
steps: Plug the meter between socket & device
Put device in standby, read the watts
details: For this check you need a simple plug-in power meter (energy cost meter).
Plug it between the socket and the device, put the device into standby and read the watts.
Many devices draw power around the clock even though they seem "off" – it adds up over the year.
A switchable power strip fully disconnects several devices at once.
Connecting a smart meter directly is planned for a future version.

summary.good: Very efficient – barely any standby use.
summary.medium: Moderate standby use – savings potential here.
summary.high: High standby use – hidden power drains at work.

room_temperature.title: Room Climate Check
room_temperature.short: Measure room temperature and find your heating savings potential.

intro.imageAlt: Illustration: person measuring the room climate with a thermometer
steps: Place a thermometer in the room
details: Place the thermometer in the middle of the room at about sitting height – not right next to a radiator, window or external wall.
Wait a few minutes for the reading to stabilise before noting it.
As a guide: about 20 °C in the living room, 18 °C in the kitchen and 16–18 °C in the bedroom.
A comfortable humidity is around 40–60 %.
Every degree less saves noticeable heating energy – without becoming uncomfortable.

status.tooCold: A bit cool – every degree less saves, but mind comfort.
status.tooWarm: A bit warm – 1 °C less noticeably cuts heating costs.
status.tooDry: Rather dry – airing out or plants can help.
status.tooHumid: Rather humid – regular airing prevents mold.

draftStatus.strong: Strong draft – checking the seals pays off.

saving.title: Potential saving
saving.context: {{percent}}% less heating energy at {{delta}} °C above {{reference}} °C – proportional for this room. Rough guide value (≈6% per °C), not a forecast.

freezer.title: Freezer Check
freezer.short: Check ice build-up and temperature to avoid wasted electricity.

intro.imageAlt: Illustration: person checking the iced-up freezer
details: Estimate the ice layer on the inner wall: from about 5 mm onwards, electricity use rises noticeably.
For the temperature, place the thermometer in the middle between the frozen items and close the door again.
Recommended is around −18 °C – colder brings hardly any benefit but costs more electricity.
Defrosting regularly saves energy and frees up space again.
Check the door seal – if it no longer closes tightly, the appliance ices up faster.

run.noFrostHint: Great – ice-free means it runs efficiently, nothing to do.
run.severityLabel: How heavy is the ice? (for the estimate)
run.energyHint: Run an energy-cost meter for a few hours before defrosting (read kWh + hours), defrost, then measure again.

method.estimate: Estimated from the ice build-up level.

summary.high: Heavy frost – defrosting now saves noticeable power.

tempStatus.tooCold: too cold – setting warmer saves power

hot_water_wait.title: Hot water wait
hot_water_wait.short: Measure how long you wait for hot water — and the potential that runs off unused.

intro.lead: Until hot water arrives, cold water often runs off unused. Find out how much.
intro.imageAlt: Illustration: person timing how long until hot water arrives
steps: Stop once it is clearly warm
details: Until hot water arrives, cold water often runs off unused – this check measures that wait.
Turn the tap fully to hot and start the stopwatch at the same moment.
Stop as soon as the water feels clearly warm.
Measure at the tap you use most often (e.g. shower or kitchen).
Long waits point to long pipe runs – a circulation line or pipe insulation can help.

run.instruction: Turn the water fully to hot, start the stopwatch — and stop as soon as it gets clearly warm.
run.stagnationHint: Measure when the pipe has cooled down – ideally in the morning before the first draw. Shortly after showering the pipe is still warm and the reading comes out too low.
run.hintStopwatch: Start the stopwatch and stop it once the water is warm.

result.explanation: In that time roughly {{liters}} L of drinking water ran off unused.
result.reuseTitle: Collected, it can be used for

furniture_spacing.title: Furniture spacing check
furniture_spacing.short: Check whether furniture or rugs are blocking your heating.

intro.lead: Unobstructed heat surfaces release their heat evenly – and the thermostat measures what it is supposed to measure. Check room by room what is in the way.
intro.imageAlt: Illustration: measuring the distance between a radiator and a sofa
details: Covered heat surfaces do not lose the heat – they release it delayed and unevenly.
The cost is indirect: an enclosed thermostat reads trapped heat, shuts off too early, and the room gets turned up by hand.
Leave roughly 10 cm of air in front of radiators so air can flow in from below.
If you have a folding rule at hand, enter the distance directly – the check then derives its rating from it.
Sofas, cabinets, long curtains or casings in front of them slow heat output.
With underfloor heating, large furniture without legs and thick rugs impede output – the system then needs a higher flow temperature.
Check each room individually – often a small rearrangement already improves heat output.

questions.furniture: Is a large piece of furniture (sofa, cabinet, shelf) standing directly in front of the radiator?
questions.cover: Is the radiator covered by a casing, curtain or shelf?
questions.valve: Is the thermostatic valve enclosed by furniture, casing or a curtain?
questions.footless: Is large furniture without legs standing flat on the floor (sofa, bed, cabinet)?
questions.carpet: Is a large, thick rug lying on the heated surface?
questions.thermostat: Is the room thermostat covered by furniture, a curtain or pictures?
questions.builtin: Is the radiator built over by fitted units, a worktop or a plinth panel?
questions.towels: Are towels or laundry hanging over the radiator?

living_room.furniture: Is a sofa, armchair or sideboard standing directly in front of the radiator?

dining_room.furniture: Is a dining table, bench or cabinet standing directly in front of the radiator?

bedroom.furniture: Is the bed, a wardrobe or a chest of drawers standing directly in front of the radiator?
bedroom.footless: Is the bed or a cabinet standing without legs directly on the heated surface?

children_room.furniture: Are the bed, shelves or toy boxes standing directly in front of the radiator?

office.furniture: Is a desk, pedestal or shelf standing directly in front of the radiator?

bathroom.carpet: Is a large bath mat permanently lying on the heated surface?

kitchen.footless: Do the fitted kitchen units sit with a closed plinth on the heated surface?

run.distanceHint: Distance between the front edge of the furniture and the radiator, level with the air inlet at the bottom. At least {{target}} cm of clear space is recommended.

summary.good: Heat surface and controls work undisturbed – exactly as intended.
summary.medium: Almost everything is clear – one point slightly slows heat output.
summary.elevated: Heat is distributed unevenly – and the controls no longer work properly.
summary.high: Heat output and controls are clearly disturbed – the room needs a higher flow temperature than necessary.

result.allClear: Nothing blocks the heat surface and the temperature sensor works freely. Worth a quick check whenever you rearrange furniture.
result.mechanism: The heat is not lost – the radiator sits inside the building envelope and releases almost all of it into the room. It costs energy in three other ways: the temperature sensor reads the trapped heat, shuts off too early, the room stays cool and gets turned up by hand. On an external wall the trapped heat raises the wall temperature and with it the loss to the outside. And a higher flow temperature is needed for the same output.

valve.why: The valve controls by the temperature it measures itself. Enclosed, it reads trapped heat instead of room temperature, closes too early, the room stays cool – and gets turned up by hand. The single most relevant finding in this check.
valve.action: Let air circulate freely around the valve head. Where that is impossible, a remote sensor or a thermostat with a detached sensor helps.

cover.why: A casing, curtain or shelf slows the airflow through the radiator and shields its radiant heat. A fixed casing weighs more than a curtain because it acts permanently.
cover.action: Shorten the curtain to windowsill height, remove the shelf. A fixed casing needs openings at the bottom and top so air can flow through.

furniture.why: Furniture directly in front deflects the warm air. The heat still reaches the room, but delayed and unevenly – and on an external wall the trapped heat warms the wall too.
furniture.action: Leave roughly 10 cm of air in front of the radiator so air can flow in from below.

footless.why: Underfloor heating releases most of its heat as radiation across the open surface. Furniture without an air gap takes that area out of service – the remaining area has to compensate with a higher flow temperature.
footless.action: Choose furniture with legs or put it on glides. Even a few centimetres of air gap help.

carpet.partly: Rug on part of the surface
carpet.yes: Thick rug on the heated surface
carpet.why: A rug acts as insulation above the heat surface. The system is designed around a low thermal resistance of the floor build-up; a thick rug exceeds it and forces a higher flow temperature.
carpet.action: Use thin rugs approved for underfloor heating – marked by the symbol or by the stated thermal resistance.

thermostat.why: The room thermostat controls the entire surface. Covered, it measures the air in its hiding place rather than the room – the surface heats too long or too briefly. With slow-responding underfloor heating this hits particularly hard.
thermostat.action: Keep the thermostat clear and uncovered, not behind a curtain, furniture or a picture. Direct sunlight and draughts distort the reading too.

builtin.yes: Radiator built over by fitted units
builtin.why: In kitchens the radiator often sits behind a plinth panel or under the worktop. This is the worst case: air cannot flow in freely, trapped heat sits permanently at the valve, and it cannot be fixed by rearranging anything.
builtin.action: Fit ventilation grilles into the plinth panel and the top cover – at the bottom for intake, at the top for outlet. When replacing the kitchen, free the radiator or switch to a plinth convector with a fan.

towels.partly: Towels over the radiator now and then
towels.yes: Towels or laundry over the radiator
towels.why: Textiles over the radiator have a double effect: they shield the heat output, and their evaporative cooling keeps the valve open longer. In a bathroom the evaporated moisture also stays in the room and has to be ventilated out.
towels.action: Do not dry wet laundry on the radiator. Mount towel rails beside rather than above the radiator; ventilate thoroughly after showering.

radiator: Keep the radiator clear – place sofa/cabinet with some distance.
No casing or long curtains in front of it.
Let air circulate freely around the thermostatic valve.
underfloor: Choose furniture with legs – an air gap to the floor helps.
Avoid large, thick rugs on the heated surface.
Prefer thin rugs suitable for underfloor heating.

result.distanceContext: At least {{target}} cm is recommended so air can flow in freely from below. Under 5 cm the air intake is effectively cut off.

notes.sensorAndCold: The room climate check measured this room below its comfort range – together with the enclosed sensor that forms a familiar pattern: the sensor reads trapped heat, shuts off too early, the room stays cool and gets turned up by hand. Freeing the sensor helps more here than any change at the thermostat.
notes.heatPump: Your profile includes a heat pump. Every blocked heat surface has to be compensated by a higher flow temperature – and with a heat pump that immediately costs efficiency. Clearing the obstruction is worth more here than with a condensing boiler.

base_load.title: Base-load check
base_load.short: Measure how much power your home draws around the clock.

intro.lead: Even with nothing actively running, your home draws power continuously – standby, fridges, router & co. This check reveals that base load.
intro.imageAlt: Illustration: person reading the base load on the electricity meter
steps: Switch off active devices – leave always-on ones (fridge, router) running
Read the power or measure briefly
intro.hint: Tip: it is most accurate at night or when nobody is actively using power.
details: Even with nothing actively running, your home draws power continuously – standby, fridges, router & co.
For the measurement, switch off all actively used devices but leave always-on ones like the fridge and router running.
Then read the power at the meter (digital meters show watts directly).
It is most accurate at night or when nobody is actively using power.
Even 20–30 watts of constant load add up to noticeable costs over the year.

modeHint.instant: Modern meters show the current power directly in watts – just read it off.
modeHint.timed: Read the meter, start the stopwatch, wait a few minutes, read again.
modeHint.ferraris: Older meters with a spinning disc: count the revolutions during the measured time.

watchHint.timed: Start, wait a few minutes, then stop.

summary.good: Your base load is low – barely any unnecessary continuous draw here.
summary.medium: Solid base load with a little room to improve.
summary.elevated: Your base load is elevated – worth checking the always-on consumers.
summary.high: High base load – a lot of power is drawn continuously. You should track down the causes.

result.note: Orientation values – base load depends on household size and appliances. This check does not count towards savings itself; the follow-up checks quantify the actual savings.
result.funnelText: Use the standby check to track down the biggest continuous consumers and see what can be switched off.

lighting.title: Lighting check
lighting.short: Find out how much switching to LED saves.

intro.lead: Old incandescent and halogen bulbs use many times more than LEDs. Check room by room what is worth it.
intro.imageAlt: Illustration: person showing smart lighting via app
details: Old incandescent and halogen bulbs use many times more energy than LEDs – at the same brightness.
Per room, count the bulbs that are not yet LED (incandescent, halogen or old energy-saving lamps).
LEDs come in every socket (E27, E14, GU10 …) and light colour – from warm white to daylight.
The switch pays off most where lights burn longest (living room, kitchen, hallway).
LEDs last far longer – saving electricity and frequent bulb changes.

run.bulbsTitle: Bulbs that are not LED yet
run.bulbsHint: For each type, count the bulbs in this room that have not been switched to LED yet.
run.hoursHint: How long is the light on here on average?

summary.good: Everything is already LED here – great, hardly anything more to gain.
summary.medium: A few bulbs could still be switched to LED cheaply.
summary.elevated: Switching to LED saves noticeable power here.
summary.high: Lots to gain here – the lighting uses unnecessarily much.

tip.good: Keep choosing warm-white LEDs when you replace bulbs.
tip.medium: Swap bulbs for LED step by step – start with the ones that are on the longest.
tip.elevated: Switching to LED clearly pays off. Mind the right socket (e.g. GU10, E27) and light colour.
tip.high: Convert these first: switching to LED usually pays for itself within a few months.

hero.title: Estimated energy costs
hero.label: Estimated energy costs / year
hero.info: This is a rough estimate based on your profile (people, living area) and the stored electricity price. With real measurements and meter readings the figure becomes much more accurate.

tips: Lower the room temperature by 1 °C – it saves about 6 % of heating energy.
Standby devices quietly draw power: switchable power strips help.
Air the room briefly with wide-open windows instead of tilting them to save heat and prevent mould.
When buying new appliances, choose the highest energy efficiency class.
Washing laundry at 30 °C instead of 60 °C saves up to two thirds of the electricity.
Set the fridge to 7 °C – any colder just wastes energy.

tips.title: Recommendations
tips.subtitle: Concrete steps for your home – no tradesperson needed, easiest first.
tips.empty: Run a few measurements first – matching tips will appear here.

standby.title: Switch off standby
standby.reason: Biggest standby item: $t(measurements.standby.deviceTypes.{{deviceType}}) at {{watts}} W. Plug those devices into a switched power strip and turn them all off with one flick.

showerhead.title: Fit a low-flow showerhead
showerhead.reason: Your showerhead delivers {{flow}} L/min. A low-flow head (~8 L/min) screws onto the hose by hand – no tools, same shower feel.

lighting.title: Switch to LED
lighting.reason: {{count}} lamps still aren't LED. Replace them one by one – start where the light burns longest each day.

hot_water_wait.title: Catch the run-off water
hot_water_wait.reason: It takes {{seconds}} s for hot water to arrive – about {{liters}} L runs off unused every time, roughly {{litersPerYear}} L over a year. Put a watering can or bucket underneath: for plants, cleaning or the toilet.

fridge.title: Turn the fridge up
fridge.reason: {{temp}} °C is colder than needed. Turn the dial down one notch – 7 °C is plenty, andeach degree warmer saves around 6 % electricity.

fridge_warm.title: Turn the fridge down
fridge_warm.reason: {{temp}} °C is too warm for safe storage. Turn the dial up one notch until you reach 5–7 °C.

freezer.title: Defrost the freezer
freezer.reason: A layer of ice drives consumption up. Switch it off, open the door, lay out towels – it costs you one afternoon.

room_temperature.title: Lower the room temperature
room_temperature.reason: {{room}} is at {{temp}} °C. Turn the thermostat back half a notch: one degree less saves around 6 % heating energy and is barely noticeable.
room_temperature.reasonNoRoom: It's {{temp}} °C here. Turn the thermostat back half a notch: one degree less saves around 6 % heating energy and is barely noticeable.

room_cold.title: Don't let the room go cold
room_cold.reason: {{room}} is at {{temp}} °C. Permanently cool rooms get damp and mould-prone. Set the thermostat to a low constant level instead of switching off and reheating later.
room_cold.reasonNoRoom: It's only {{temp}} °C here. Permanently cool rooms get damp and mould-prone. Set the thermostat to a low constant level instead of switching off and reheating later.

humidity_high.title: Air out against damp
humidity_high.reason: {{room}} is at {{humidity}} % humidity – too high. Air out two to three times a day for 5 minutes with the window wide open, instead of leaving it tilted.
humidity_high.reasonNoRoom: Humidity is at {{humidity}} % – too high. Air out two to three times a day for 5 minutes with the window wide open, instead of leaving it tilted.

humidity_low.title: The air is too dry
humidity_low.reason: {{room}} is at {{humidity}} % humidity – very dry, which irritates the airways. Shorter airing and not overheating usually does it.
humidity_low.reasonNoRoom: Humidity is at {{humidity}} % – very dry, which irritates the airways. Shorter airing and not overheating usually does it.

draft.title: Seal the draught
draft.reason: {{room}}: there's a noticeable draught at a window or door. Self-adhesive sealing tape from the hardware store presses straight into the frame – peel, press, done.
draft.reasonNoRoom: There's a noticeable draught at a window or door. Self-adhesive sealing tape from the hardware store presses straight into the frame – peel, press, done.

furniture_spacing.title: Clear the radiator
furniture_spacing.reason: Furniture or curtains sit too close and trap the heat. Move them back a little – from about 30 cm the warmth reaches the room.

base_load.title: Track down constant draws
base_load.reason: Your base load is {{watts}} W – even with nothing running on purpose. The standby check shows you device by device where it comes from.

consumption_up.title: More $t(monitoring.energyTypes.{{carrier}}) than last year
consumption_up.reason: Your meter readings show {{percent}} % more consumption than the same period last year – about {{amount}} {{unit}} extra. That is measured, not estimated. Find the cause before it adds up over another year.

tips.allHandled: All handled – nice! New measurements will surface fresh recommendations here.
